sections.html: The tiger lotus (Nymphaea zenkeri) is a bulb plant with broad, wavy-edged leaves and a variegated colour pattern. It has two kinds of leaves: completely submersed, somewhat heart-shaped leaves that grow near the bulb, and floating leaves on long, thin stems that look like lily pads resting at the surface. Some tiger lotuses grow primarily green leaves with red variegation, whereas others have red leaves with darker, reddish-purple striping.

Planting: the bulb arrives in a plastic pot covered in rock wool. Small leaves sprouting from the bulb are often damaged in transit or may melt away after planting, but a healthy bulb is the most important part. Remove the bulb from the pot and rock wool, and rinse off any debris. Tiger lotuses get rather large, so plant it in the midground or background. Gently push one-third of the bulb into the substrate so that the shoots or leaves are completely above ground. Do not bury the entire bulb or it will rot. If the bulb floats at first, wait for it to become waterlogged enough to sink. As the roots grow into the substrate, they will firmly anchor the bulb.

Growing: once well established, it quickly grows plenty of big leaves, so feed it with comprehensive fertilisers such as Easy Green and Easy Root Tabs. To bring out the red colour, provide medium to high lighting with some extra iron fertiliser.

Pruning: the plant may grow so many floating leaves that it blocks light from other plants. To trim, clip the lily pad at the base of its stem, closest to the bulb. Continuously pruning a few floating leaves keeps the plant from growing too tall and makes it grow bushier.

The tiger lotus can grow flowers at the surface. If it has lots of lily pads, it may produce a flower with colours ranging from white to yellow. When the flower wilts, it may develop into multiple seeds that can be collected. Another method is via the bulb: if the plant is doing well, the parent bulb may form small daughter bulbs that can be detached and replanted in another aquarium.

Sometimes bulb plants have a dormant period, where all the leaves die off and leave just the bulb. One option is to keep the bulb in the tank; after several months it will start sprouting new leaves. You can also take the bulb out, keep it in a damp container for several months, and then put it back into the tank, after which new leaves will sprout and begin growing again.
